title: App-based financial incentives to encourage naloxone carriage
official: Contingency management to increase naloxone carriage: development and testing of a new behavioural intervention (CM4COYN)
summary:
Background and study aims
Naloxone is a medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose and save a person’s life. Take-home naloxone (THN) is provided to people who use opioids so that they, their friends, family or other people nearby can use it in an emergency.

However, having naloxone available does not necessarily mean that people carry it with them when they are away from home. This means that naloxone may not be available when it is needed. Research has found that rates of naloxone carriage are low, despite naloxone being widely available.

Contingency management (CM) is an approach that uses rewards to encourage specific behaviours. This study will develop and test a mobile phone-based contingency management intervention (mCM) designed to encourage people to carry their take-home naloxone when they are away from home.

The study has three main aims: to develop the mobile intervention, to find out whether it is acceptable, usable and reliable for people who use opioids, and to assess whether it is feasible to carry out a larger study in the future.

Who can participate?
Adult patients aged 18 years and over who use opioids and have been supplied with take-home naloxone.

What does the study involve?
In the main feasibility study, 40 participants will be randomly allocated to one of two groups – app + financial incentives or app only.

Participants in both groups will receive naloxone training and use the app. Participants in the intervention group will receive notifications when they leave their home. They will be asked to use their smartphone camera to verify that they are carrying their naloxone. If they successfully verify that they are carrying it, they will receive a £2 reward through the app. If they are not carrying their naloxone, they will be asked to select a reason and will receive a £1 reimbursement.

Participants in the control group will use the app and receive naloxone training but will not receive the prompts during the intervention period.

All participants will be asked about their experience of the study and will complete follow-up assessments at 6 and 10 weeks. These will include questions about naloxone carriage, treatment and drug use, as well as their experience of using the app. Interviews will normally take place remotely by telephone or Microsoft Teams, although participants can request a face-to-face interview at the participating clinic. Participants will be reimbursed for their time spent taking part in the study interviews.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not receive a direct personal benefit from taking part. However, taking part may help researchers understand whether a mobile phone-based intervention could help increase naloxone carriage. The findings may help inform the development of a larger study and future approaches to improving access to naloxone during an opioid overdose.
Participants in the intervention group may also receive financial rewards when they successfully verify that they are carrying their naloxone.

The study is not expected to involve significant physical risks. However, some participants may experience emotional or psychological discomfort when discussing naloxone carriage, opioid use or related experiences. There may also be some burden associated with receiving notifications, using the application or experiencing technical problems.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being run by King’s College London in collaboration with South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust.
Participants will be recruited through NHS and non-NHS drug treatment and harm reduction services in London and Derby. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
March 2025 to March 2027 2026. 

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
1. Dr Nicola Metrebian, Co-Chief Investigator and Reader in Addiction Treatment Research, King’s College London, nicola.metrebian@kcl.ac.uk
2. Professor John Strang, Co-Chief Investigator, King’s College London.

Inclusion criteria:
1.	Aged 18+ years of age
2.	Able to  provide written informed consent

4.	Individuals who use opioids
